title: Probability flow ODEs in score-based and reflected diffusion models

paper.title: Probability flow ODEs in score-based and reflected diffusion models
paper.abstract: Abstract Probability-flow ordinary differential equations (PF-ODEs) are widely used as deterministic samplers for score-based diffusion models. Their usual justification is that the Fokker–Planck equation of a diffusion can be rewritten as a continuity equation driven by the score function of the forward diffusion. This identity does not, however, guarantee that the resulting velocity field generates a well-posed flow. We provide theoretical insights into the design of such deterministic samplers for generative models based on diffusions and reflected diffusions. We identify sufficient conditions for a regular Lagrangian PF-ODE flow to exist; reverse sampling and invertibility require two-sided divergence control. For learned scores, sampler stability is controlled by an unweighted velocity error, exposing a mismatch with density-weighted score matching and motivating architectural control of Jacobians, divergence, growth, and compression. Under the manifold hypothesis, positive-time regularization justifies an early-stopped PF-ODE while constants deteriorate near the data endpoint; an explicit sphere example shows that the exact deterministic flow becomes singular as the noise level vanishes even though the diffusion marginals remain well defined. These theoretical insights translate into concrete design principles for stable, invertible, and constraint-preserving diffusion samplers. We illustrate the practical relevance of these design principles using controlled numerical experiments.

sections.heading: 1 Probability-flow ODEs in diffusion models
sections.text:
Score-based diffusion models [ 19 ] generate data by reversing a noising process and may be sampled either with a reverse-time SDE [ 3 , 5 ] or with the deterministic probability-flow ODE (PF-ODE) introduced in Song et al. [18] . The PF-ODE is attractive because it removes stochastic simulation, supports deterministic encoding/decoding, and permits likelihood calculations [ 19 , 18 ] . In constrained generative modeling, reflected diffusion models [ 15 , 12 ] keep the forward process inside a prescribed domain and can likewise be paired with a deterministic PF-ODE. It is then tempting to conclude that the ODE Z ˙ t = v ⁡ ( Z t , t ) \dot{Z}_{t}=v(Z_{t},t) automatically transports p 0 p_{0} to p t p_{t} . This conclusion is not automatic [ 7 ] : the PDE ( 2 ) determines an Eulerian density evolution, whereas a deterministic sampler requires a Lagrangian flow of individual samples. A unique and smooth density flow can exist even when the associated PF-ODE fails to generate a regular Lagrangian flow from the data time [ 7 ] . This distinction is especially relevant under the manifold hypothesis [ 10 ] i.e. when data law is supported on a lower-dimensional manifold.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: We use theoretical insights from [ 7 , 8 ] to derive implications for the design and training of score-based and reflected diffusion models, and exhibit explicit examples and sampler diagnostics. First, when data is supported on a lower dimensional manifold, positive-time diffusion regularizes the singular data law but the PF-ODE may become singular as t ↓ 0 t\downarrow 0 . In Section 3 we give an explicit example of this type, which leads to collapse of the normal directions at the data endpoint. This complements convergence results for diffusion models under the manifold hypothesis [ 10 , 4 , 17 ] . Second, for learned scores, deterministic sampler stability depends not only on score-matching error but also on regularity, divergence, growth, and compression of the induced velocity field. Third, for reflected models, the PF-ODE contains no explicit reflection term: confinement follows from tangency of the probability-flow velocity, rather than from a zero-normal-score condition. These observations lead to a common design principle: the PF-ODE should be treated as a learned dynamical system with its own well-posedness and conditioning requirements, rather than as an automatic consequence of score estimation. In particular, early stopping, velocity-field regularization, divergence control, low-density validation, and appropriate boundary constraints should be viewed as structural components of deterministic diffusion sampling. We illustrate these principles with numerical experiments (Section 6 and Appendix B.1 ), with a focus on endpoint conditioning, the DSM–velocity-error gap, and Jacobian regularization.

sections.heading: 2.1 Marginal matching requires a Lagrangian flow
sections.text: The identity between ( 2 ) and the continuity equation establishes that p t p_{t} is an Eulerian solution for the velocity ( 3 ). To obtain a sampler one needs a flow map Z ⁡ ( t , ⋅ ) Z(t,\cdot) whose trajectories solve Z ˙ = v ⁡ ( Z , t ) \dot{Z}=v(Z,t) which transports p 0 p_{0} to p t p_{t} . (4) For non-smooth velocity fields the relevant object is a regular Lagrangian flow (RLF), which permits Sobolev or bounded-variation (BV) spatial regularity while imposing a quantitative compressibility bound. Under local BV regularity of the drift and score, linear growth, and a one-sided bound on the negative divergence of v v , such a unique RLF exists and satisfies ( 4 ) [ 7 , 11 , 1 ] . This is substantially weaker than assuming a globally Lipschitz score. The distinction matters for model validation. A well-posed SDE and a unique Fokker–Planck density do not certify the PF-ODE. The diffusion benefits from stochastic regularization, whereas the deterministic dynamics directly inherit score singularities. For a Brownian forward process initialized by the uniform law on an interval, for example, p t p_{t} is smooth and strictly positive for every t > 0 t>0 , yet the score outside the initial support behaves as O ⁡ ( 1 / t ) O(1/t) as t ↓ 0 t\downarrow 0 ; the PF-ODE has no regular Lagrangian flow from time zero [ 7 ] . Thus “the score is smooth for every positive time” is weaker than the time-integrated regularity needed by the sampler.

sections.heading: Design implication: early stopping is structural.
sections.text: Under the manifold hypothesis linear VP/VE forward diffusions regularize the law at every δ > 0 \delta>0 . On [ δ , T ] [\delta,T] the score has explicit Hessian, divergence, and linear-growth bounds sufficient for PF-ODE well-posedness, with constants that deteriorate as δ ↓ 0 \delta\downarrow 0 [ 7 ] . The principled deterministic pipeline is therefore μ 0 → forward diffusion p δ → PF-ODE on ​ [ δ , T ] p T , p T → reverse PF-ODE p δ , \mu_{0}\xrightarrow{\text{forward diffusion}}p_{\delta}\xrightarrow{\text{PF-ODE on }[\delta,T]}p_{T},\qquad p_{T}\xrightarrow{\text{reverse PF-ODE}}p_{\delta}, (5) and the final passage p δ → μ 0 p_{\delta}\to\mu_{0} requires a limiting argument or a separate terminal denoising step. Reducing δ \delta improves endpoint fidelity but worsens conditioning. This gives an analytic interpretation of the empirical difficulty of the final denoising steps and suggests treating the truncation time as a model-design parameter, not merely an ODE-solver tolerance.

A model intended only for one-way generation may tolerate weaker divergence control than a model intended as an invertible continuous normalizing flow. Architectural and regularization choices should therefore be aligned with the required downstream operation.

sections.heading: Codimension one.
Relation to convergence results under the manifold hypothesis.
sections.text: De Bortoli [10] showed that denoising diffusion models can converge to targets supported on lower-dimensional manifolds or empirical measures and obtained quantitative W 1 W_{1} guarantees without assuming an ambient target density. Azangulov et al. [4] obtain score-learning and reverse-SDE sampling rates largely independent of ambient dimension, while Potaptchik et al. [17] showed that the number of reverse-SDE discretization steps required for KL convergence can scale linearly, up to logarithmic factors, with intrinsic dimension. These are distributional convergence results for stochastic diffusion samplers. Proposition 1 addresses a different question: whether the associated deterministic probability flow remains a regular and invertible ambient-space flow as the noise level vanishes. The sphere example shows that, even with the exact score, approaching a lower-dimensional target forces collapse of normal directions. Thus favorable intrinsic-dimensional sampling rates do not imply Lagrangian regularity, bounded compression or invertibility of the PF-ODE at t = 0 t=0 .

sections.heading: Design implication.
sections.text: Under the manifold hypothesis, when the target distribution is idealized as being exactly supported on a lower-dimensional manifold, the zero-noise limit should be viewed as a singular collapse limit , rather than as an ordinary well-conditioned ODE time. If stable deterministic transport, invertible encoding/decoding, or change-of-variables likelihood evaluation is required, a natural strategy is to stop the PF-ODE at some δ > 0 \delta>0 and treat the passage from p δ p_{\delta} to the data distribution separately, for example through a terminal denoising or manifold-valued correction step. If reverse trajectories are integrated closer to zero, one should expect normal Jacobian factors and ambient volume elements to collapse, while the conditioning constants of the deterministic flow deteriorate even for a perfect score. This is an intrinsic geometric consequence of removing diffusion regularization, not merely an effect of score-estimation error.

sections.heading: Design implication: architecture should enforce regularity.
sections.text: The learned flow must control more than pointwise error. Sufficient conditions include local W 1 , p W^{1,p} regularity ( p > 1 p>1 ), a one-sided divergence bound for v θ v_{\theta} , and linear growth. These quantities are not controlled by density-weighted score matching alone. Practical mechanisms suggested by the theory include spectral normalization, Jacobian penalties, explicit divergence regularization, and uniform control of network growth. For a sequence of increasingly accurate score models, compression and growth constants must remain uniformly bounded; otherwise E θ → 0 E_{\theta}\to 0 does not imply convergence of the samplers. This implication complements statistical score-estimation guarantees [ 13 ] and convergence analyses that assume smooth PF-ODE dynamics [ 14 ] and also connects to schedule design [ 6 , 16 ] . A schedule optimized only for score-estimation difficulty or terminal SNR may be poorly conditioned for deterministic transport near the data endpoint.

sections.heading: 5.2 Endpoint and boundary failure modes
sections.text: Two failure mechanisms clarify what a constrained sampler must control.

sections.heading: Data-endpoint singularity.
sections.text: Reflected Brownian motion started from a compactly supported density inside an interval has a unique smooth positive density for every t > 0 t>0 and satisfies tangency at the walls, yet the score in the initial vacuum still behaves like 1 / t 1/t [ 8 ] . The PF-ODE has no regular Lagrangian flow from time zero, while it is well posed on every [ δ , T ] [\delta,T] [ 8 ] . Thus reflection does not cure the data-endpoint pathology; early stopping remains necessary for compactly supported data.

sections.heading: Boundary-current compression.
sections.text: For more general no-flux density–flux pairs, if the density degenerates at the boundary then p ​ v ⋅ ν = 0 p\,v\cdot\nu=0 no longer implies v ⋅ ν = 0 v\cdot\nu=0 . A boundary current can coexist with exact marginal transport and confined integral curves while producing unbounded compression and no regular Lagrangian flow [ 8 ] . Uniformly elliptic reflected VE/VP models after positive-time regularization avoid this mechanism because their densities are positive up to the boundary, but the example is a warning for learned constrained flows: preserving mass and keeping sample paths inside the domain are not sufficient for the stability of the deterministic sampler. Geometry also enters through score regularity. Smooth convex domains are favorable for Neumann/co-normal regularity, whereas nonconvex or nonsmooth boundaries can degrade second-derivative estimates near the wall [ 8 ] . Domain choice and boundary representation are therefore part of the conditioning of a reflected score model, not merely semantic constraints on the output space.

sections.heading: 6 Implications: Design principles for diffusion samplers
sections.text: These results suggest treating the PF-ODE as a learned dynamical system, not a by-product of score estimation. The central object is the learned probability-flow velocity, not the score in isolation.

sections.heading: 6.2 Use density-stratified validation
sections.text: The inverse-density factor in ( 16 ) suggests that global denoising-score-matching is a poor diagnostic for ODE sampling. A more informative report stratifies validation points into bins according to log ⁡ p t ​ ( x ) \log p_{t}(x) or another proxy for density and evaluates score and velocity/Jacobian error in each bin. The same principle applies at the boundary of a constrained domain: evaluate tangency and compression as a function of distance to ∂ Ω \partial\Omega . Such diagnostics target regions that density weighting tends to hide.

sections.heading: Numerical illustration
sections.text: In the Gaussian example above, we perturb the score by a localized bump of width w = 0.2 w=0.2 , centered either at x 0 = 0 x_{0}=0 or at the low-density location x 0 = 4 x_{0}=4 , and choose the amplitudes so that both perturbations have the same integrated DSM error E θ 2 = 10 − 3 E_{\theta}^{2}=10^{-3} . Despite identical DSM loss, the tail perturbation produces a 12.3 × 12.3\times larger unweighted velocity error, a 152 × 152\times larger excess Jacobian penalty, and a 15.9 × 15.9\times larger mean endpoint trajectory error on a uniform validation grid (Figure 1 a). Thus a global density-weighted score metric can make two models appear equivalent while density-stratified or trajectory-level diagnostics distinguish their PF-ODE behavior. Trajectory-level tests are also important. If Z θ Z_{\theta} is used for deterministic decoding or likelihood evaluation, one should test forward–reverse round trips, sensitivity to score perturbations, and volume distortion along trajectories. These are aligned with properties controlled by regular Lagrangian-flow theory and can distinguish a low-loss score estimator from a stable ODE vector field.

sections.heading: 6.3 Choose schedules together with the endpoint cutoff
sections.text: For compactly supported data, early-stopping estimates depend on accumulated noise variance ς t 2 \varsigma_{t}^{2} . In the VE case ς t 2 ≍ t \varsigma_{t}^{2}\asymp t , representative score-Hessian bounds scale like ς t − 2 + R 2 ​ ς t − 4 \varsigma_{t}^{-2}+R^{2}\varsigma_{t}^{-4} , so integrated conditioning deteriorates rapidly as the sampler is extended toward t = 0 t=0 . The relevant design variable is therefore the pair (noise schedule, endpoint cutoff) rather than either one alone. A schedule that injects enough noise to regularize the score quickly can make a given positive cutoff better conditioned, while an aggressive reduction of δ \delta can erase this benefit. This perspective is complementary to recent schedule-design work based on Lipschitz conditioning [ 6 ] .

For reflected models the same principle interacts with geometry. Parabolic regularization gives a smooth positive density up to a smooth boundary, but constants depend on boundary regularity and can deteriorate at corners or nonconvex singularities. If the constraint set is a modeling choice, a smooth geometric representation can therefore improve score regularity and deterministic sampling. These design principles, summarized in Table 1 , suggest that validation protocols for ODE-based diffusion models should, in addition to score loss and sample-quality metrics, evaluate: (i) the time profile of Jacobian/divergence norms of v θ v_{	heta} ; (ii) empirical volume compression along trajectories; (iii) sensitivity of the sampler to decreasing δ \delta ; (iv) score/velocity errors stratified by density level; and, for constrained models, (v) the boundary residual | v θ ⋅ ν | |v_{	heta}\cdot
u| . These diagnostics target quantities that affect the flow and can reveal failures invisible to density-weighted training loss. The results also separate two modeling choices that are often conflated. The reverse SDE is a stochastic process whose score error is naturally averaged under its evolving law, while the PF-ODE is a deterministic vector field whose global trajectories can be affected by low-density regions. A score architecture and schedule optimized for SDE sampling need not be optimal for ODE sampling. If deterministic decoding, fast ODE generation, or exact likelihoods are central goals, PF-ODE conditioning should be included explicitly in training and schedule selection.

sections.heading: Appendix A Some mathematical results on ODE samplers for diffusion models
sections.text: This appendix summarizes results from [ 7 , 8 ] . For mathematical definitions we refer to Ambrosio [2] .

sections.heading: A.1 PF-ODE in the whole space
sections.text: Consider ( 1 ) with scalar uniformly nondegenerate σ ⁡ ( t ) ≥ σ min > 0 \sigma(t)\geq\sigma_{\min}>0 , and let p t p_{t} be its marginal density. Suppose the drift is locally bounded variation (BV) in space with integrable growth, its distributional divergence is absolutely continuous with an integrable one-sided L ∞ L^{\infty} bound, and the score ∇ log ⁡ p t \nabla\log p_{t} has corresponding Sobolev/BV regularity, linear growth, and an integrable upper bound on Δ ​ log ⁡ p t \Delta\log p_{t} . Then the velocity ( 3 ) generates a unique regular Lagrangian flow and transports p 0 p_{0} to p t p_{t} . If the opposite sign of ∇ ⋅ v \nabla\cdot v is also integrably bounded in L ∞ L^{\infty} , the time-reversed regular Lagrangian flow exists and is the a.e. inverse of the forward flow. For linear VP/VE diffusions with compactly supported initial law, no density or score at time zero is required: for each δ > 0 \delta>0 , Gaussian regularization yields the required score bounds on [ δ , T ] [\delta,T] . In the VE scaling ς t 2 ≍ t \varsigma_{t}^{2}\asymp t , worst-case bounds grow polynomially in δ − 1 \delta^{-1} , which explains the deterioration toward the data endpoint.

sections.heading: A.2 Learned-score stability
sections.text: Let Z δ Z^{\delta} and Z θ δ Z_{\theta}^{\delta} be the exact and learned regular Lagrangian flows, both initialized as the identity at time δ \delta . Under local W 1 , p W^{1,p} regularity ( p > 1 p>1 ), growth, and compression bounds, for x x in a ball B r B_{r} one obtains an estimate of the form ℒ d ​ ( { x ∈ B r : | Z δ ​ ( T , x ) − Z θ δ ​ ( T , x ) | > η } ) ≤ C p + L θ ​ E v / λ log ⁡ ( 1 + η / λ ) , \mathcal{L}^{d}\!\left(\left\{x\in B_{r}:\left|Z^{\delta}(T,x)-Z_{\theta}^{\delta}(T,x)\right|>\eta\right\}\right)\leq\frac{C_{p}+L_{\theta}E_{v}/\lambda}{\log(1+\eta/\lambda)}, (25) where E v E_{v} is defined in ( 14 ), L θ L_{\theta} is the compression constant of the learned flow, and C p C_{p} depends on the Sobolev norm of the exact velocity on a confinement ball. Taking λ = E v \lambda=\sqrt{E_{v}} yields convergence in measure as E v → 0 E_{v}\to 0 with fixed regularity/compression constants. Equation ( 16 ) relates E v E_{v} to the denoising score-matching loss.

sections.heading: A.3 PF-ODE in a bounded domain
sections.text: Let Ω ⊂ ℝ d \Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a bounded smooth domain and consider the normally reflected diffusion ( 17 ). Its probability flux is J = f p − 1 2 σ 2 ∇ p J=fp-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}\nabla p . If, on [ δ , T ] [\delta,T] , p p is positive up to the boundary and the velocity v = J / p v=J/p has the interior/collar BV regularity [ 9 ] and one-sided divergence bounds required for a regular Lagrangian flow [ 2 ] , then the no-flux condition gives a vanishing normal trace of v v . Extending v v by zero outside Ω \Omega introduces no singular boundary divergence term, and the resulting RLF stays in Ω ¯ \overline{\Omega} and transports p δ p_{\delta} to p t p_{t} . For C 2 , α C^{2,\alpha} domains and sufficiently regular drift, parabolic boundary regularity verifies these conditions for every δ > 0 \delta>0 and arbitrary initial law. The reflected VE and VP diffusions used in constrained score-based modeling satisfy the resulting early-stopped transport statement. The constants degenerate as δ ↓ 0 \delta\downarrow 0 .

sections.heading: Appendix B Practical checklist for a PF-ODE implementation
sections.text: For an implementation intended to use deterministic PF-ODE sampling, the theory motivates the following checks in addition to ordinary score-model evaluation: 1. report the data-endpoint truncation δ \delta and the terminal denoising procedure; 2. measure Jacobian/divergence norms of v θ v_{\theta} over time and across density quantiles; 3. test sensitivity of sample trajectories and likelihood estimates to the ODE solver and to perturbations of s θ s_{\theta} ; 4. if invertibility is used, test both forward and reverse compression rather than forward generation alone; 5. for reflected models, evaluate v θ ⋅ ν v_{\theta}\cdot\nu on boundary samples and use the drift-dependent co-normal target; 6. stratify score error by density level so that tail or boundary errors are not hidden by density weighting.

sections.heading: B.1 Numerical experiments
sections.text: We report three numerical experiments that isolate the mechanisms behind the design principles. Exact reference scores allow us to distinguish score approximation, flow conditioning, and numerical integration error.

sections.text: DSM calibration uses trapezoidal quadrature with 501 501 time nodes and 16001 16001 spatial nodes on [ − 8 , 8 ] [-8,8] ; E v E_{v} and J err J_{\rm err} use 30001 30001 spatial nodes on [ − 6 , 6 ] [-6,6] , and K J K_{J} uses 100001 100001 nodes. The regression experiment uses NumPy’s default random generator with seed 42 42 . The regularization test uses a known reference score and a single coefficient.
